Friday, 11 pm.
Salma and I finally sat down after yesterday's blow-up about the kitchen. We made a rule before starting: you say the other person's point back first. It felt silly. Salma went first: "You're saying you feel like you're the only one who notices the mess, and it makes you feel used." That was exactly it. Then I had to do hers: "You're saying you get home at nine, exhausted, and my nagging makes the flat feel like a second office." She nodded. I also said sorry for calling her lazy, which was the worst thing I said. She said sorry for "control freak". Then we wrote a rota on the back of an electricity bill and stuck it on the fridge. Mine: Mondays and Thursdays. Small. But it's on paper.
— Kiran

qa.q: Where did Kiran and Salma write the rota?
qa.a: They wrote a rota on the back of an electricity bill and stuck it on the fridge.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when Salma repeated Kiran's point back?
qa.a: Kiran felt understood, because Salma's words were "exactly it".

qa.q: Why is the rota on the fridge a useful end to the repair?
qa.a: It turns good feelings into a plan both can check, so the next messy night has an answer that doesn't depend on mood.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt when Kiran described her tiredness at nine?
qa.a: Salma probably felt seen for the first time in the argument, which made it easier to apologise for "control freak".

grounding: Shows flatmates restating each other's point, owning their harshest words, and ending with one practical agreement, a written rota.
